ann_30.original: Fixed-defect gate. The unit opens for patients whose thallium scan shows a fixed defect and stays shut for everyone else: it acts on 15 of the 15 fixed-defect patients (share 100%) and on 0 of the other 227 training patients. High fasting blood sugar nearly closes it: for the typical patient with a fixed defect its value is 2.73 with fasting sugar of 120 mg/dL or less and 0.15 above it. When open it pulls predicted risk down. Over the fixed-defect patients it changes the log-odds by -2.42 on average and the predicted risk by -0.215 (probability, with the gate minus without it); its own edge to the output carries -2.09 of that log-odds change and its feed into the heart-rate unit -0.33. In the whole model, for the typical patient with normal fasting sugar, predicted risk is 16% with a normal scan, 2% with a fixed defect and 37% with a reversible defect. The direct edge of the normal-scan indicator (-0.54 per sd) scores both defect types above a normal scan (log-odds -0.55 for a reversible defect against -1.63 for a normal scan), and the gate then takes the fixed-defect log-odds down to -4.12, so the model places a fixed defect below a normal scan. This is fitted to 15 rows (5 of them with high fasting sugar), whose training outcome rate is 60%; their mean predicted risk is still 57% because their direct terms are high (mean 3.27 log-odds above the training average). The gate reads as a correction of the linear terms for this small group, not as evidence that a fixed defect lowers risk. The closed form is attached as formula evidence (coefficients rounded to three significant figures; off by up to 0.0015 on the training rows).

High fasting blood sugar weakens it: for that typical patient, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL rather than 120 mg/dL or less raises the predicted risk through this part from about 81% to about 99%.

ann_31.original: Atypical-angina hinge. The unit is on for patients with atypical angina and off for the rest: it acts on 42 of the 42 training patients with atypical angina (share 100%) and on 0 of the other 200. The atypical-angina indicator has no direct edge, so this unit is that level's own route to the output; it lowers the log-odds of those patients by a small amount: switching it off changes their log-odds by -0.113 and their predicted risk by -0.0098 on average (with minus without). In the whole model chest-pain type also acts through the direct edges of the other levels: for the typical patient predicted risk is 16% with no chest pain (asymptomatic), 9% with atypical angina (unit value 0.94), 2% with non-anginal pain and 1% with typical angina (unit value 0.00). Switching the unit off moves training AUC from 0.9424 to 0.9422: a near-negligible refinement that slightly lowers atypical-angina risk. Described more than explained: it is a fixed offset for one chest-pain level.

ann_32.original: Direct linear terms, the additive backbone. Each input here reaches the output through its own edge, so each moves the log-odds by a fixed amount per sd of its z-scored value. The largest weights (per sd): number of major vessels coloured by fluoroscopy 2.16; a flat ST segment 1.08; male sex 0.85 on the male indicator and -0.48 on the female indicator; non-anginal pain -0.76; serum cholesterol 0.68; typical angina -0.66; resting blood pressure 0.57; a normal thallium scan -0.54; ST depression 0.53; high fasting blood sugar -0.53; exercise-induced angina 0.34; no chest pain 0.30; an upsloping ST segment -0.20; maximum heart rate -0.20; age 0.10; normal fasting sugar 0.007. Prediction: vessel count is the strongest single driver. For the typical patient predicted risk is 16% with no vessels, 69% with one, 96% with two and above 99% with three. High fasting blood sugar lowers predicted risk through its direct edge: for the typical patient with a normal scan, from 16% to 4% in the whole model (the fixed-defect gate is shut in both cases). That direction is worth checking: among the 33 training patients with high fasting sugar the outcome rate is 45%, against 44% for the other 209. ann_33.original: Fixed-defect and heart-rate pathway (serial composition). The fixed-defect gate has two copies: one goes straight to the output, the other is added into a heart-rate unit that also reads maximum heart rate and the ST-T abnormality indicator of the resting ECG. The heart-rate unit is passed to the output through a second unit that is on for 242 of the 242 training patients (share 100%), so on the training data that second unit is a rescaled, shifted copy of the heart-rate unit. Prediction: a higher maximum heart rate lowers predicted risk, and the slope steepens once the heart-rate unit switches on. For the typical patient the unit is off (value 0.00) at 130 beats per minute and on (value 0.27) at 140 beats per minute; in the whole model predicted risk falls from 27% at 90 beats per minute to 20% at 130 beats per minute (direct edge alone), 19% at 140 beats per minute and on to 10% at 200 beats per minute (direct edge plus the unit); in log-odds that is -1.02, -1.37, -1.48 and -2.22 at those four points. Switching the whole pathway off (gate shut, the rescaled unit held at its training mean) moves training AUC from 0.9424 to 0.9342; for the 227 patients without a fixed defect it changes mean predicted risk by 0.0015, so outside the fixed-defect group the heart-rate unit is a small refinement of heart rate's direct edge.

parts.name: heart_disease_risk
parts.original_hypothesis: Root. The predicted risk is the sigmoid of a sum: the direct linear terms, the fixed-defect pathway's two exits and the atypical-angina hinge each add to the log-odds through their own edge into the output; the parts do not multiply or gate one another at the output, and the one serial link is the fixed-defect gate feeding the heart-rate unit inside the pathway. The one-hot columns for a normal resting ECG, left ventricular hypertrophy, no exercise angina, a downsloping ST segment and the thal codes for a reversible defect and level four have no edge; because each categorical variable is one-hot and z-scored, their levels still change the prediction through the other levels' indicators (a reversible defect moves the prediction through the normal-scan indicator). Prediction: the parts add on the log-odds scale, so a fixed defect shifts the log-odds by a gap that does not depend on vessel count. For the typical patient the log-odds with a normal scan are -1.63, 0.79, 3.21 and 5.63 for no to three vessels, and with a fixed defect -4.12, -1.70, 0.72 and 3.14; on the risk scale the fixed-defect patient with three vessels is still at 96%. By ablation the direct terms carry most of the ranking (training AUC 0.9424 falls to 0.6906 when they are replaced by their mean), then the pathway (0.9342 without it), the gate (0.9347) and the hinge (0.9422).

The largest weights (per sd): number of major vessels coloured by fluoroscopy 2.16; a flat ST segment 1.08; male sex 0.85 on the male indicator and -0.48 on the female indicator; non-anginal pain -0.76; serum cholesterol 0.68; typical angina -0.66; resting blood pressure 0.57; a normal thallium scan -0.54; ST depression 0.53; high fasting blood sugar -0.53; exercise-induced angina 0.34; no chest pain 0.30; an upsloping ST segment -0.20; maximum heart rate -0.20; age 0.10; normal fasting sugar 0.007. Prediction: vessel count is the strongest single driver. For the typical patient predicted risk is 16% with no vessels, 69% with one, 96% with two and above 99% with three. High fasting blood sugar lowers predicted risk through its direct edge: for the typical patient with a normal scan, from 16% to 4% in the whole model (the fixed-defect gate is shut in both cases). That direction is worth checking: among the 33 training patients with high fasting sugar the outcome rate is 45%, against 44% for the other 209. Replacing the whole part by its training mean moves training AUC from 0.9424 to 0.6906 and flips 80 predictions, so most of the model's ranking of patients comes from these terms. The full linear sum is attached as formula evidence (coefficients rounded to three significant figures; off by up to 0.0098 on the training rows).

parts.name: fixed_defect_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Fixed-defect gate. The unit opens for patients whose thallium scan shows a fixed defect and stays shut for everyone else: it acts on 15 of the 15 fixed-defect patients (share 100%) and on 0 of the other 227 training patients. High fasting blood sugar nearly closes it: for the typical patient with a fixed defect its value is 2.73 with fasting sugar of 120 mg/dL or less and 0.15 above it. When open it pulls predicted risk down. Over the fixed-defect patients it changes the log-odds by -2.42 on average and the predicted risk by -0.215 (probability, with the gate minus without it); its own edge to the output carries -2.09 of that log-odds change and its feed into the heart-rate unit -0.33. In the whole model, for the typical patient with normal fasting sugar, predicted risk is 16% with a normal scan, 2% with a fixed defect and 37% with a reversible defect. The direct edge of the normal-scan indicator (-0.54 per sd) scores both defect types above a normal scan (log-odds -0.55 for a reversible defect against -1.63 for a normal scan), and the gate then takes the fixed-defect log-odds down to -4.12, so the model places a fixed defect below a normal scan. This is fitted to 15 rows (5 of them with high fasting sugar), whose training outcome rate is 60%; their mean predicted risk is still 57% because their direct terms are high (mean 3.27 log-odds above the training average). The gate reads as a correction of the linear terms for this small group, not as evidence that a fixed defect lowers risk. The closed form is attached as formula evidence (coefficients rounded to three significant figures; off by up to 0.0015 on the training rows).

parts.name: fixed_defect_heart_rate_pathway
parts.original_hypothesis: Fixed-defect and heart-rate pathway (serial composition). The fixed-defect gate has two copies: one goes straight to the output, the other is added into a heart-rate unit that also reads maximum heart rate and the ST-T abnormality indicator of the resting ECG. The heart-rate unit is passed to the output through a second unit that is on for 242 of the 242 training patients (share 100%), so on the training data that second unit is a rescaled, shifted copy of the heart-rate unit. Prediction: a higher maximum heart rate lowers predicted risk, and the slope steepens once the heart-rate unit switches on. For the typical patient the unit is off (value 0.00) at 130 beats per minute and on (value 0.27) at 140 beats per minute; in the whole model predicted risk falls from 27% at 90 beats per minute to 20% at 130 beats per minute (direct edge alone), 19% at 140 beats per minute and on to 10% at 200 beats per minute (direct edge plus the unit); in log-odds that is -1.02, -1.37, -1.48 and -2.22 at those four points. Heart rate enters the unit with weight 0.94 per sd, the unit reaches the output with weights 0.98 and then -0.089, and heart rate's own direct edge weighs -0.20 per sd. The unit is off for 52 training patients; 52 of them have a maximum heart rate below 140 bpm. The ST-T abnormality indicator enters the unit with weight -0.43 per sd and holds it off for the 2 of 2 training patients with that ECG finding, a regime of 2 rows. Partner: the gate's copy enters the unit with weight 2.18, so for a typical patient with a fixed defect the unit stays on across the whole sweep (value 4.11 at 90 beats per minute, 8.74 at 200 beats per minute) and adds to the gate's direct pull. Switching the whole pathway off (gate shut, the rescaled unit held at its training mean) moves training AUC from 0.9424 to 0.9342; for the 227 patients without a fixed defect it changes mean predicted risk by 0.0015, so outside the fixed-defect group the heart-rate unit is a small refinement of heart rate's direct edge.

parts.name: atypical_angina_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Atypical-angina hinge. The unit is on for patients with atypical angina and off for the rest: it acts on 42 of the 42 training patients with atypical angina (share 100%) and on 0 of the other 200. The atypical-angina indicator has no direct edge, so this unit is that level's own route to the output; it lowers the log-odds of those patients by a small amount: switching it off changes their log-odds by -0.113 and their predicted risk by -0.0098 on average (with minus without). In the whole model chest-pain type also acts through the direct edges of the other levels: for the typical patient predicted risk is 16% with no chest pain (asymptomatic), 9% with atypical angina (unit value 0.94), 2% with non-anginal pain and 1% with typical angina (unit value 0.00). Switching the unit off moves training AUC from 0.9424 to 0.9422: a near-negligible refinement that slightly lowers atypical-angina risk. Described more than explained: it is a fixed offset for one chest-pain level.

For a typical patient it acts on, it lowers the predicted risk of heart disease from about 99% without this part to about 81% with it (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 15 training patients (patients the part acts on).
In the training data, 9 of these 15 patients had heart disease.

The model has little data on this: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan).
